report.summary: Incident S03 is INCONCLUSIVE per the system determination: contradicting evidence was 36% of weighed evidence against a 35% maximum, so no root cause is asserted. The leading candidate (H1, confidence 0.60) is a consumer-side failure in notification-worker: heap exhaustion with GC thrash from 09:30, TemplateCache.put OutOfMemoryErrors from 09:54, and OOMKills at 09:55, 10:10 and 10:25. Queue lag onset falls between 09:55 and 10:00 and grew to 946.91 s by 10:30, coinciding with a drop in worker request_rate from about 30 to about 6 req/s. Producer rate and queue metrics were unavailable, so the lag growth cannot be reconciled with intake and the drop may be a consequence of the crashes. H2 (v1.8.0 in-process template cache as leak source, confidence 0.40) and H3 (email-provider eu-west latency, confidence 0.12) remain unresolved, with H3 not fully ruled out.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: Heap pressure built from about 09:00 (81% to 99%), with GC thrash from 09:30 and a TemplateCache.put OutOfMemoryError at 09:54:22 followed by OOMKill at 09:55:02. The restart cut consumption from about 30 to about 6 req/s, and the queue lag then grew from about 4 s to 947 s by 10:30 as the restart loop repeated.
assumptions: The producer rate stayed near its prior level, since order-service and notification-queue have no metrics
The heap climb is a real leak or unbounded growth rather than a transient load effect

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: The v1.8.0 in-process template cache, deployed 2026-08-31, grows without bound, possibly keyed per recipient, and drives the heap climb that ends in repeated OOM in TemplateCache.put. The 2026-09-02 batch-size increase from 50 to 100 may accelerate this growth, so the lag would recur until the cache is bounded or the change is rolled back.
assumptions: TemplateCache is the dominant allocator, which the stack trace only shows as the failure point
The v1.8.0 cache change is the source of the growth, which is supported by timing only

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: Elevated eu-west latency at the email provider would slow sends and back up consumption, producing lag. Its warnings began at 09:08 and do not cluster at the 10:00 onset, and the intake drop coincides with the OOM kill, so this is at most a secondary factor.
assumptions: The status page reflects the path used by notification-worker
Send slowness would reduce consumption rather than only increase per-message time

inferred_conclusions.statement: The lag is most likely driven by a consumer-side failure in notification-worker: GC thrash, TemplateCache OOMs and OOMKill restart loops stalled consumption while the queue continued to fill.
The 09:55 drop in request_rate is most likely a consequence of the worker crash and restart rather than a cause of the lag, since M31 measures worker processing rather than queue arrival.
Upstream volume growth is unlikely to explain the lag, since checkout-service and api-gateway traffic was flat; this is indirect because no order-arrival metric exists.
A v1.8.0 template cache leak is a candidate source of heap growth, but the cache mechanism is unobserved and the 50-to-100 batch-size change is untested.
Email-provider latency is at most a secondary or background contributor, since its warnings began before the lag and do not cluster at the 10:00 onset.

remediation.action: Extend health checks to exercise queue consumption and send-path latency, and add metrics for notification-queue and email-provider.

findings.summary: notification-worker lag onset is between 09:55 and 10:00 UTC. queue_lag_s was flat at about 4 s through the 09:55 sample, then jumped to 141 s at 10:00 and rose roughly 130 s per 5 minutes to 947 s at 10:30. observations.statement: queue_lag_s was normal (3.86–4.16 s) at every sample from 09:00 to 09:55, then 140.92 s at 10:00:00, 273.18 s at 10:05, 404.28 s at 10:10, 533.97 s at 10:15, 660.01 s at 10:20, 823.97 s at 10:25 and 946.91 s at 10:30. Onset is therefore between 09:55 and 10:00 UTC.

interpretations.statement: The lag is most likely a consumer-side failure in notification-worker. Heap exhaustion from GC thrash starting around 09:30 led to OOMKills at 09:55, and the restarts cut consumption to about 20% of the prior rate. Lag then grew at roughly 2 s per s.

The lag-growth rate is consistent with consumption below the arrival rate. The producer rate was not measured, but a steady intake of about 6 req/s against an earlier 30 req/s suggests the producer did not drop, so the worker's consumption fell.

email-provider slowness is probably a secondary or background factor. Its 2400 ms warnings predate the lag and persist after the memory recovery, and there is no matching error-rate or latency change in notification-worker.

The TemplateCache.put OOM may be a memory leak or unbounded cache growth. This is suggested by the heap climbing steadily for 30+ minutes and failing in the same method every time, but it is not confirmed by the data here.
